extracted.intended_audience: DHS adjudicators, immigration officers, immigration applicants and advocates (stakeholders commenting on public charge rule)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural guidance for determining whether an applicant is "likely at any time to become a public charge," including which public benefits are considered (cash assistance for income maintenance and long-term institutionalization), how to treat disability and institutionalization evidence, burden of proof, and related administrability and policy considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits considered for public charge
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider receipt of public cash assistance for income maintenance and long-term institutionalization at government expense when assessing whether an applicant is likely at any time to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS focuses on benefits most indicative of primary dependence on the government for subsistence and excludes most non-cash and supplemental benefits from the public charge inadmissibility determination. This approach is intended to identify applicants who are likely to become primarily dependent on the government for subsistence without interfering with the administrability and effectiveness of other benefit programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government source neutrality for cash assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of government is not limited to the Federal government; DHS will not distinguish between cash assistance solely because of the source of the funds (Federal vs State, Tribal, territorial, or local).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State, Tribal, territorial, and local cash assistance for income maintenance are included in consideration because such assistance can be indicative of primary dependence on the government for subsistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of guaranteed income programs
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider 'guaranteed income' programs if they typically do not provide the primary source of income for recipients or are made available without income-based eligibility rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a program does not function as cash assistance for income maintenance (i.e., not means‑tested or not a primary subsistence source), DHS would not treat participation in that program as indicative of being a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of tax credits (EITC and CTC)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS is declining to include Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) and Child Tax Credit (CTC) in the definition of public cash assistance for income maintenance, and is not including tax credits in the calculation of gross annual household income for public charge purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons include that many with moderate or higher incomes are eligible, the practical difficulty distinguishing refundable portions versus liability‑offsetting portions, potential spousal/joint return attribution issues, and a desire to avoid confusion or fear around tax filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-cash benefits generally excluded (SNAP, Medicaid, CHIP, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most non-cash, supplemental, or special-purpose benefits are not included in the definition of public charge because they generally are less indicative of primary dependence on the government for subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS relied on benefits-granting agencies (e.g., USDA stating SNAP is supplementary; HHS stating Medicaid (except long‑term institutionalization) is not indicative of primary dependence). DHS also cites documented chilling effects from including non-cash benefits in prior rulemaking (reduced enrollment, adverse public health outcomes) as a reason to exclude such benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term institutionalization at government expense is a considered factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Current or past long-term institutionalization at government expense will be considered as bearing on whether an individual is likely to become primarily dependent on the government for subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term institutionalization is treated as one of the core scenarios relevant to the public charge statute. DHS will consider such institutionalization in the totality of the circumstances, but it is not alone dispositive. Home- and community-based services (HCBS) are not considered long-term institutionalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of unlawful or inappropriate institutionalization (ADA/Olmstead issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider evidence that past or current institutionalization was in violation of Federal law (e.g., the ADA, Section 504, Olmstead v. L.C.) as part of the totality of the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may submit evidence that institutionalization was improper or violative of disability rights; DHS will consider such evidence as a guardrail. DHS declined to shift the burden of proof to the agency; applicants must submit the evidence. DHS also will provide officer training on how to consider disability and evidence of rights violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant bears burden to submit evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant for admission or adjustment of status bears the burden of proof to establish eligibility for the immigration benefit sought and must submit evidence (including evidence that institutionalization violated Federal law) as part of the public charge determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will not adopt commenters' suggestion to remove the regulatory text requiring evidence be submitted by the applicant or to shift evidentiary burdens to the agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fixed numerical time threshold for 'long-term' institutionalization
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not adopt a specific length-of-stay threshold (e.g., 30 days, 5 years) to define 'long-term' institutionalization; there is no definitional standard in Medicaid or other benefit programs that supports a specific numerical threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead DHS (in collaboration with HHS) will develop sub‑regulatory guidance to assess evidence. Relevant considerations may include duration of institutionalization, whether the person was assessed/offered and declined HCBS, and the availability of such services in the individual's geographic area. Permanent or indefinite institutionalization is most likely to contribute to inadmissibility, but indefinite or shorter institutionalizations may also qualify depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disability not alone sufficient to find public charge
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider disability, by itself, to be sufficient evidence that an applicant is likely to become a public charge and will not presume disability alone negatively impacts other public charge factors in 8 CFR 212.22.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officer training will cover how to consider disability in the totality of circumstances and make clear that disability does not automatically imply poor health, likelihood of cash assistance receipt, or likely need for long-term institutionalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting and totality of circumstances approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Receipt of cash assistance for income maintenance or long-term institutionalization are evidence that, in the totality of the circumstances, may indicate primary dependence; however, such evidence is considered as part of the overall analysis and is not dispositive by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will evaluate current and past behavior and other factors consistent with statutory guidance and prior agency practice to predict future likelihood of becoming a public charge. The rule emphasizes focusing on indicators most probative of primary dependence to avoid undue interference with important benefit programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy and administrability considerations in defining benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: In defining which benefits to consider for public charge purposes, DHS takes into account policy goals such as clarity, fairness, national resilience, administrability, and foreseeable chilling effects on benefit uptake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS cites evidence of chilling effects from the 2019 Final Rule (e.g., reductions in Medicaid and CHIP enrollment) and considers the public health and economic consequences of expanding the set of benefits considered. DHS disavows using the rule as a tool to deter persons not subject to the public charge ground from accessing benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and statutory context informs scope of consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS relies on Congressional precedent and prior agency practice distinguishing between cash and non-cash benefits (e.g., IRCA, 1999 Interim Field Guidance) and interprets statutory terms consistent with agency discretion left by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency considers Congress's past distinction between cash and non-cash benefits and subsequent amendments that limited application in certain populations, supporting the agency's authority to specify which public benefits are relevant for public charge determinations.
